newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate urged to approve European arms accord.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate urged to approve European arms accord.

text.p: The Clinton administration urged the Senate on Tuesday to give swift approval to changes negotiated in a European military forces treaty following the breakup of the Soviet Union and Warsaw Pact.
They said Senate failure to approve the agreement by May 15 could endanger prospects of agreement on adapting the basic 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe treaty to post-Cold War conditions.
The agreement was negotiated following Russian complaints that treaty constraints on deployment of conventional weapons restricted its ability to meet security requirements in the north Caucasus.

Undersecretary of State Lynn Davis told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee that unless the Senate approved the agreement by May 15 the issue could be reopened, precluding agreement on basic elements of adapting the CFE treaty -- part of an effort to pave the way for enlargement of the NATO alliance.
Republican Sen. Gordon Smith of Oregon, chairing the hearing, accused the administration of making "frenzied efforts" to renegotiate the treaty on terms acceptable to Russia.

He said further steps were needed to strengthen the security of neighbouring countries that would be affected by changes in deployment of Russian forces. He said Moldova, Ukraine and Georgia had yet to approve of the agreement.
But Davis said the agreement was essential to their security. She denied the agreement gave Russia the right to station troops in neighbouring states without their consent.
Administration submission of the so-called flank agreement for Senate approval stemmed from negotiations with key senators on the Chemical Weapons Convention approved by the Senate last Thursday.

The administration had said the flank agreement merely amended an existing treaty and Senate approval was not required. But it agreed to submit it as part of a deal to win Senate consideration of the chemical weapons treaty.
